title: FTC settles with DoNotPay over unsubstantiated 'AI lawyer' service claims
description: On 25 September 2024, the US Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement with DoNotPay, Inc., which had marketed itself as offering 'the world's first robot lawyer' and an AI service capable of generating legal documents and substituting for a human lawyer. The FTC alleged DoNotPay could not substantiate claims that its service's output was comparable to advice from a human lawyer, and had not tested its performance against the standard a licensed attorney would provide, nor employed or retained attorneys to ensure the accuracy and quality of the legal documents it generated. DoNotPay agreed to pay $193,000, notify subscribers of certain products of the settlement and its limitations, and was barred from making similar unsubstantiated claims going forward.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion. Reuses the DEC-022/PAT-020/CTR-022/EVI-020/BRD-020 AI-output-verification cluster established by the Mata v. Avianca incident, since this is the same failure to verify AI-generated professional output against a competence standard, at a company-product scale rather than a single filing.

root_cause: DoNotPay marketed its AI-generated legal document and advice service as comparable to a human lawyer without testing that claim or employing attorneys to verify the accuracy and quality of the AI-generated output before it reached consumers.

citations.title: DoNotPay Settles FTC Allegations that it Deceived Consumers about the AI 'Lawyer' Service it Claims Can Substitute for Actual Legal Consultations

relationships.reason: Verifying AI-generated legal document output against a professional accuracy standard before offering it to consumers addresses exactly the deficiency the FTC identified.
This incident extends the AI-output-verification question to a commercial product making professional-substitute claims at scale.
